CHAPTER 10: SECULAR OR NON-RELIGIOUS WORLDVIEWS

LEARNING OUTCOMES
- Identify three key moments in the emergence of an independent secular values system (the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, Existentialism).
- Show how communal values can be shaped by sources other than religion (sport, feminism, the law).
- Describe three different ways in which religions relate to secular culture (Laudato si', education, marriage).

KEY TERMS
- Religious values: values inspired by belief in God or gods.
- Secular values: non-religious values.
- Secular culture: the shared values, knowledge and social practices influenced by a non-religious worldview.
- Existentialism: a philosophical theory that stresses the existence of the individual as a free and responsible agent, deciding their own development through acts of free will.
- Individualism: a worldview that values the power of reason and the uniqueness of the person above all else.
- Communal values: values held by a group of people, e.g. people from the same country, community, village or organisation.
- Feminism: the advocacy (support) of women's rights on the grounds that the sexes are equal.
- Secular: a non-religious way of understanding human existence; a worldview that makes no reference to God, gods or the sacred.
- Secularisation: the change of a society from close identification with religious values and institutions towards non-religious values and secular institutions.
- Secularism: 'a desire to cut the links between religion and values'. It places human beings at the centre of everything and values human reason above all else.
- Humanism: a philosophy or worldview which says there is nothing higher or other than human existence.

INTRODUCTION
- Chapter 5 noted that the religious response to life's great questions is not the only response.
- All cultures, without exception, trace their roots back to mythic or religious worldviews, but these have since been challenged by other ways of approaching life's great questions.
- Various alternative worldviews have produced values, and these values have shaped the communities and cultures they came from.
- Sometimes these worldviews oppose religious worldviews; sometimes there is a degree of harmony between them.

KEY MOMENT 1: THE RENAISSANCE (FIFTEENTH AND SIXTEENTH CENTURIES)
- Secularism can be traced back to the Renaissance in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
- The Renaissance was a period of huge innovation and change in art, music, literature, architecture, economics, philosophy and religion.
- It began in Italy and gradually spread throughout Europe.
- Of special interest: the emergence of humanism.
- Renaissance humanism was characterised by individualism. It placed human beings at the centre. Each individual was seen as unique and special and as possibly able to understand the world.
- It valued the power of reason and the uniqueness of human beings above all else. This focus on the individual is still common in today's society.
- Confidence in human potential and belief in human reason led to enormous creativity in all areas of life.
- The most outstanding achievements were in scientific discovery. Modern scientific discoveries can be traced back to the growth of scientific reasoning and secular humanism in the Renaissance.
- Desiderius Erasmus was a key thinker of the Renaissance (studied in Chapter 5).
- Exam tip: use Erasmus as an example of a Renaissance humanist when writing about the emergence of a secular values system.

KEY MOMENT 2: THE ENLIGHTENMENT (EIGHTEENTH CENTURY)
- A period in European history when a group of thinkers proposed a new way of viewing the world. Like the Renaissance, its theories influenced how society found meaning and created values.
- Took place mainly in the eighteenth century, when philosophers in England, Scotland, France and Germany built a worldview in response to the social and political situation in Europe.
- These thinkers wanted to break free from what they saw as the immature position of blind faith in the Church and other authorities.
- They believed humankind itself, through reason, should decide how life should be lived.
- Motto: 'Have the courage to know'.
- The most intense and important period was between the English Revolution (1688) and the French Revolution (1789).
- Birth of the 'coffee house' as a place to meet and share opinions on many subjects.
- Big increase in publications such as pamphlets and literary magazines, which helped open debate and thought. New forms of literature and drama appeared.
- Class barriers broke down: in coffee houses and salons (bars) it became fashionable to ignore differences in social status. This contrasted with the Court of the King, where only the nobility could attend.
- Exam tip: you can use Descartes (Chapter 2) to illustrate Enlightenment values.

THE EMERGENCE OF HUMAN RIGHTS
- Motto of the French Revolution: 'Liberty, Equality and Fraternity'. These aims came to be seen as rights - human rights. The idea of human rights took shape in this period.
- Thomas Paine: the best-known political writer of the late eighteenth century. Involved in the American Revolution (1773-83) and the French Revolution (1789-92).
- Paine's two important books: The Age of Reason (a description of the century as a whole) and The Rights of Man (one of the major themes of the period). They greatly influenced the human rights movement in Europe and America.
- 1789: the National Assembly of France approved the Declaration on the Rights of Man and the Citizen - one of the founding documents of the human rights tradition. It grew out of the Enlightenment, where reason and liberty came together.
- It became the model for much of Europe and for the Constitution of the United States of America.
- Its introduction says ignorance or contempt of the rights of man is 'the sole cause of public calamities', so it sets out 'the natural, unalienable, and sacred rights of man'.
- It contains seventeen rights or articles, considered essential to the happiness of all.
- First article: 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may be founded only on the general good.'
- This can be compared with the first article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights passed by the United Nations. (The book says 'after World War I'; the UN Declaration was in fact adopted after World War II - the photo shows Eleanor Roosevelt holding a poster of it in New York in November 1949.)
- The humanism of the Enlightenment continues in the worldview and values of the United Nations declaration.

KEY MOMENT 3: EXISTENTIALISM (TWENTIETH CENTURY)
- One of the most influential philosophies of the twentieth century (its founder was mentioned in Chapter 2).
- World War I (1914-1918): around twenty million deaths and a further twenty million casualties. The first time the world had seen such large-scale carnage and violence.
- Its impact on the next generation cannot be underestimated. Many were disillusioned and no longer cared for the values of the previous generation. They did not look to the Church for meaning; they believed they only had themselves in the quest for meaning.
- The post-war age was marked by discontent.
- Starting point of existentialism: the existence of the individual as a free and responsible agent, deciding their own development by free will.
- Central concerns: the freedom to choose one's own life, and the dangers of making the wrong choice.
- Jean-Paul Sartre (1905-1980): a prominent figure in French politics and public life in the 1960s and a strong supporter of existentialism.
- Famous quote: 'Man is condemned to be free.' Dilemma: if the person alone is responsible for their life, they cannot find any meaning from outside. This worldview was bleak - all anyone has is the fact of their existence.
- Responsibility: Sartre said the person is called to take up the fact of their existence, commit to living, and take full responsibility for that decision. This seems a contradiction: if there is no meaning, why bother?
- Each person is responsible for their choices and must decide for or against an action and take responsibility. There are no criteria for deciding right and wrong.
- Existentialism rejects the possibility of meaning outside the person; it completely rejects all other possible meanings.
- It made an important contribution to secular humanism today. Its stress on the individual and distrust of 'meaning' from other sources like religion has had an enormous impact on the values of contemporary Western societies.
- Quote: '[Life is] full of loneliness, and misery, and suffering, and unhappiness, and it's all over much too quickly.' - Woody Allen.
- Exam tip: you can include Nietzsche (Chapter 2) to develop your answer.
- Sample exam question: profile how any two moments (e.g. the rise of humanism, existentialism) contributed to non-religious communal values. (40 marks)

HOW COMMUNAL VALUES CAN BE SHAPED BY SOURCES OTHER THAN RELIGION
- A religious worldview finds meaning and value through faith in the divine and transcendent - God.
- A secular worldview does not look for meaning outside the person, yet it has produced important values and shares values with religious worldviews: equality of all people, dignity of human life, tolerance and compassion.
- But some secular values are at odds with some religious convictions and values.
- Three non-religious sources of communal values: sport, feminism, the law.

SOURCE 1: SPORT
- Sport is a prominent social institution in almost every society.
- Almost every parish in Ireland has a GAA club - over 2,500 clubs on the island of Ireland. Most communities also have soccer, golf and tennis clubs.
- James H. Frey and D. Stanley Eitzen, in their journal article 'Sport and Society', recognise sport's unique influence: 'No other institution, except perhaps religion, commands the mystique, the nostalgia, the romantic ideational cultural fixation that sport does. No other activity so paradoxically combines the serious with the frivolous, playfulness with intensity, and the ideological with the structural.'
- Parents, teachers and community leaders encourage children into sport young, as an effective way to learn values and character traits.
- Values sport teaches: self-discipline, sportsmanship, appreciation of hard work, competition, teamwork, goal-setting and attainment.
- Sport can be a huge source of national or communal pride, e.g. a county reaching an All-Ireland final: cars, houses, pubs and schools decorated in county colours; talk dominated by the game and the scramble for tickets. Sport can bring a community together and teach us to value our communities.
- Liam Griffin, manager of the Wexford hurling team, 1996: on the way to Dublin to play Offaly in the Leinster hurling final, he stopped the bus on the Wexford-Wicklow border and made a famous speech, then had the team walk in silence out of Wexford.
- Speech themes: 'Who are you?'; tradition and pride in the county's proud past; 'You come from a fighting tradition'; 'It is only for seventy minutes'; 'Today we are playing for a way of life'; 'We are the boys of Wexford who fought with heart and hand.'
- That year Wexford won both the Leinster final and the All-Ireland final.
- Griffin never mentioned skills, techniques, goals or points. He spoke of history, tradition, pride and family, so the players played for their people, families and community.
- Kellie Harrington, Olympic gold medal winner, in an interview with the Irish Times: boxing all over Ireland has taken many kids off the street; they may not all be champions but they have made something of their lives because they were taught discipline in the boxing club. Coaches are 'unpaid, voluntary life-skills coaches' who work full-time jobs and have families yet still choose to help the kids of their community.
SOURCE 2: FEMINISM
- The Enlightenment brought great change; humanism gave a renewed sense of human potential. Ideas of tolerance, equality, natural rights and education rights flourished before the French Revolution. Feminism (the women's movement) began in this context.
- Modern feminism can be traced to around the French Revolution. Women were involved at all levels of society, but in the Declaration on the Rights of Man and the Citizen only men were considered citizens. Again and again the cause of equality for women was ignored in battles for liberation.
- Olympe de Gouges (1748-1793) wrote the Declaration on the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen in 1791, in response to the Declaration on the Rights of Man. She called for better education rights and equal rights within marriage for women. This inspired others.
- Mary Wollstonecraft (1759-1797), in England, published A Vindication of the Rights of Women in 1792.
- In 1793 all women were barred from political activity in France and Olympe de Gouges was guillotined. The revolution did not include equality for women.
- World War I changed women's lives dramatically: when men went to war, women took up their roles with energy and courage. After the war, women in many countries won the right to vote.
- Women in Ireland were legally entitled to vote on the same terms as men from the founding of the Irish Free State in 1922.
- Feminism has many strands, but they are united by concern for the quality of life of families, women, men and children.
- It brought the values of equality to political, social and personal life. It promoted the value of lived experience in making judgements. It allowed women to speak about their lives in a way unheard of before the twentieth century.
- Women's voices needed to be heard where laws were made: marriage, inheritance, property, political involvement, childcare and child labour.
- Today women and men still seek equality in pay, employment and political representation. Childcare and access to education affect all genders.
- Ireland and Europe have equality legislation protecting all members of society.
- European Commission's EU Gender Equality Strategy 2020-2025, launched March 2020: aims for a more gender-equal Europe by 2025 - 'a Union where women and men, girls and boys, in all their diversity, are free to pursue their chosen path in life, have equal opportunities to thrive, and can equally participate in and lead our European society.'
- Feminism was one of the movements that led to such laws and strategies.
- Emma Watson, 2014 speech to the United Nations as ambassador for the global equality movement HeForShe: feminism is not just a women's issue - inequality is felt by both men and women in different ways.

SOURCE 3: THE LAW
- A country's legal system tells us a lot about its values: who makes laws, how laws are decided, the court system, who runs it, and how laws are enforced, regulated and monitored.
- Ireland values equality: two pieces of legislation set out equality rights and outlaw discrimination - the Employment Equality Acts 1998-2015 and the Equal Status Acts 2000-2015.
- They outlaw discrimination in employment, vocational training, advertising, collective agreements (contracts between employers and unions) and the provision of goods and services.
- Nine grounds on which discrimination is unlawful: gender; civil status (married or single); family status (having children or not); sexual orientation; religion; age (does not apply to a person under 18); disability; race; membership of the Traveller Community.
- Marriage equality: the Thirty-fourth Amendment of the Constitution (Marriage Equality) Act 2015 allowed marriage between two persons without distinction as to their sex. Approved at a referendum on 22 May 2015. Before this, same-sex marriage was illegal in the Republic of Ireland. The Act states no religious body is obliged to recognise a particular form of marriage ceremony, and no religious solemniser must solemnise a marriage not recognised by their religious body.
- Abortion: a 2018 referendum amended the Constitution to allow the Oireachtas (the legislature of Ireland) to legislate for abortion. Passed on 25 May 2018; signed into law by the president in October 2018.
- These two amendments marked a significant shift in values and attitudes in Ireland. Many other countries followed, especially on same-sex marriage.

THREE WAYS RELIGIONS RELATE TO SECULAR CULTURE

EXAMPLE 1: LAUDATO SI'
- Published by Pope Francis in 2015: Laudato si' (On Care for Our Common Home).
- Addressed to 'every single person living on this planet' - the first and only time a papal encyclical has been addressed to all people, not just Catholics.
- Pope Francis urges us to listen to 'the cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor'.
- December 2015: international leaders met in Paris to secure a global climate deal - the Paris Agreement. Many hoped Laudato si' would be a voice of influence; it offered a powerful message for the negotiations.
- Pope Francis criticised weak leadership: 'It is remarkable how weak international political responses have been' (LS, 54).
- To prepare, he engaged in dialogue with scientists and was advised by the Pontifical Academy of Sciences.
- Trócaire appointed a dedicated Laudato si' officer to help communities explore environmental issues.
- Many parishes set up Laudato si' book clubs in response to 'Truly much can be done!' (LS, 180).

EXAMPLE 2: EDUCATION
- In Ireland, just over 90% of primary schools and 50% of secondary schools are under Catholic patronage.
- Bishop Donal McKeown, address 'The Churches and Education - Context, Vision and Values': the Catholic Church has its own schools as 'a privileged means of promoting the formation of the whole person', since the school is where 'a specific concept of the world, of the human person, and of history is developed and conveyed'.
- Historically, religious congregations and dioceses provided sites and money for school buildings and often taught free of charge.
- Catholic primary schools are linked to the local parish and hand on Christian values, including preparation for Sacraments. They are also regulated by the Department of Education and Skills through the national curriculum.
- From the mid-2000s many religious congregations transferred their second-level schools to lay education trust bodies:
- CEIST (Catholic Education and Irish Schools' Trust): brought together orders like the Mercy and Presentation Sisters.
- ERST (Edmund Rice Schools' Trust): took over the Christian Brothers' schools.
- Le Chéile Schools Trust: formed by other smaller congregations.
- This ensured the schools would keep a religious ethos in future. The trusts are run by lay people and follow civil law and canon law (Church law). Ireland is the only country to replace religious orders with lay trusts.
- Vision 08 - A Vision for Catholic Education in Ireland (Irish bishops): Catholic education aims to develop each student's full potential, the whole person, including the fundamental questions about the meaning of life, and through students to transform wider society.

EXAMPLE 3: MARRIAGE
- Marriage is a civil (legal) contract, whether in a place of worship or a registry office. In a place of worship the civil element must also be fulfilled.
- Agreement between religious institutions and the State in Ireland: a religious leader (e.g. a priest) can act as a civil registrar, overseeing both the civil contract and the religious covenant of marriage.

rows.prompt: The development of non-religious communal values can be traced back to moments such as the rise of humanism and existentialism. Profile how any two such moments contributed to the development of non-religious communal values.
rows.model_answer:
The Renaissance (fifteenth and sixteenth centuries) began in Italy and spread through Europe, bringing change in art, music, literature, architecture, economics, philosophy and religion. Secularism, 'a desire to cut the links between religion and values', can be traced to this time. Renaissance humanism held that there is nothing higher than human existence and was marked by individualism: each person was unique and able to understand the world, and reason was valued above all. This confidence led to great creativity, especially in science. Desiderius Erasmus was a key humanist. The focus on the individual is still common today.

Existentialism arose in the twentieth century after World War I (1914-1918), which killed around twenty million people. Many were disillusioned, rejected the previous generation's values and no longer looked to the Church for meaning; they believed they only had themselves. Existentialism sees the individual as a free and responsible agent deciding their own development by free will. Jean-Paul Sartre said 'Man is condemned to be free': we cannot find meaning outside ourselves, must take full responsibility for our choices, and there are no criteria for right and wrong. Its stress on the individual and distrust of meaning from religion made an important contribution to secular humanism and has had an enormous impact on contemporary Western values.

rows.prompt: Outline how the idea of human rights emerged during the Enlightenment.
rows.model_answer:
The Enlightenment took place mainly in the eighteenth century, when philosophers in England, Scotland, France and Germany wanted to break free from blind faith in the Church and other authorities. They believed humankind, through reason, should decide how life is lived; the motto could be summed up as 'Have the courage to know'. People debated in coffee houses and salons regardless of social status, and pamphlets and magazines spread new ideas.

From this came the French Revolution's motto 'Liberty, Equality and Fraternity', aims that came to be seen as human rights. Thomas Paine, the best-known political writer of the time, wrote The Age of Reason and The Rights of Man, which greatly influenced the human rights movement in Europe and America. In 1789 the National Assembly of France approved the Declaration on the Rights of Man and the Citizen, with seventeen articles. Its first article states: 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.' It became a model for much of Europe and for the US Constitution, and its humanism continues in the United Nations' Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

May refer to: reason over blind faith; 'Have the courage to know'; coffee houses and breaking class barriers; 'Liberty, Equality and Fraternity'; Thomas Paine and his two books; 1789 Declaration (17 articles, first article); model for Europe and US Constitution; link to UN Universal Declaration.

rows.prompt: Using the examples of sport, feminism and the law, show how communal values can be shaped by sources other than religion.
rows.model_answer:
Communal values are values held by a group gathered for a common purpose, and they can be shaped by non-religious sources.

Sport: almost every Irish parish has a GAA club, with over 2,500 on the island. Frey and Eitzen say no institution 'except perhaps religion' has sport's mystique. Sport teaches self-discipline, sportsmanship, hard work, teamwork and goal-setting, and brings pride, as when a county reaches an All-Ireland final. In 1996 Liam Griffin's speech to the Wexford hurlers spoke of history, tradition, pride and family, not skills; Wexford won Leinster and the All-Ireland. Kellie Harrington says boxing coaches are 'unpaid, voluntary life-skills coaches'.

Feminism: it began around the French Revolution, when only men were citizens. Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration on the Rights of Woman (1791) and Mary Wollstonecraft A Vindication of the Rights of Women (1792). After World War I many women won the vote; in Ireland from 1922. Feminism brought equality into political, social and personal life and led to laws such as the EU Gender Equality Strategy 2020-2025.

The law: a country's laws show its values. Ireland's Employment Equality Acts and Equal Status Acts outlaw discrimination on nine grounds, including gender, religion and membership of the Traveller Community. The 2015 marriage equality referendum and 2018 abortion referendum showed a significant shift in Irish values.

rows.prompt: Describe two ways in which religion relates to secular culture.
rows.model_answer:
Laudato si': In 2015 Pope Francis published Laudato si' (On Care for Our Common Home), addressed to 'every single person living on this planet' - the first and only encyclical addressed to all people, not just Catholics. He urged us to hear 'the cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor' and criticised how weak international political responses to climate change had been. He prepared by talking with scientists and was advised by the Pontifical Academy of Sciences. It offered a powerful message during the Paris Agreement talks in December 2015 and still influences the climate conversation; Trócaire appointed a Laudato si' officer and parishes set up book clubs.

Education: just over 90% of Irish primary schools and 50% of secondary schools are under Catholic patronage. Historically, religious congregations provided sites, money and free teaching. Catholic schools hand on Christian values and prepare children for Sacraments, but are regulated by the Department of Education and Skills through the national curriculum. Since the mid-2000s, congregations have transferred schools to lay trusts like CEIST, ERST and Le Chéile, so religious ethos continues under lay management following civil and canon law.
